metaphor.sentence: Three wheels must line up before the lock will open — income, obligations and evidence.

proposition: While the affordability assessment runs, assembling turns the wait into the assessment — so the customer answers once and the assessor gets a complete file.

duration.note: Nectar's own marketing states a 7-minute application and 97% same-day funding.

wait.whyItExists: Before it can lend, the lender must form a view on suitability and affordability. That view needs evidence, and gathering evidence takes time.
wait.todayItFeelsLike: A form. Then silence. Then a decision you cannot interrogate.

asks: One question at a time, sized for a tap — never an eighteen-field form.
“Is the $9,400 card the only balance you're consolidating?”
“Did your hours change in the last three months?”
learns: Which of the declared expenses are fixed and which are seasonal.
Where stated income and bank-feed income disagree, and why.
Whether consolidation actually reduces total cost, or just moves it.
prepares: A structured affordability file the assessor would otherwise assemble by hand.
The suitability rationale, written against the Responsible Lending Code.
The two questions the assessor would have had to email back and ask.
resolves: Discrepancies the customer can clear in the moment, instead of a day later.
The document chase — nothing is requested that has already been supplied.

reward.headline: A decision you can read, not just receive.
reward.detail: At the end of the wait the customer gets the assessor's actual reasoning — what was counted as income, what was treated as a fixed cost, and what would need to change for a different answer. If the answer is no, they leave knowing exactly what would make it yes.

permission.consent: You agreed to a bank feed and a credit check for this application.
reads: What you told us in the application
hardStops: It never makes or communicates a credit decision.
It never contacts a third party on your behalf.
It never keeps the bank feed after the application closes.
permission.ipp3aNotice: Your credit file comes from a credit reporter, not from you. Under the Privacy Act 2020 we tell you that we collected it, why, who sees it, and how to correct it — on this screen, not in a policy page.
permission.retention: The bank feed is deleted when the application closes. The assessment record is kept for seven years, as lending records must be.

human.gateAt: before any credit decision is formed or communicated
human.whyStatutory: CCCFA lender responsibility principles — the lender, not a tool, must be satisfied the loan is suitable and affordable.

primary.mechanism: The customer answers a handful of short questions during a wait they were already having, instead of an eighteen-field form before it.

secondary.metric: quality of the file at decision
secondary.mechanism: Discrepancies are resolved while the customer is still present, so the assessor opens a complete file instead of starting an email thread.

evidencePack.example: bank feed (90 days), credit file, stated income
childcare treated as a fixed cost; overtime excluded from income
assessor reinstated $180/wk overtime after Mere confirmed it is contracted

persona.name: Mere
persona.context: Consolidating a $9,400 credit card balance. Hamilton. Applied at 9:14am.

steps.showsCustomer: Your assessment has started. It usually finishes today. While it runs, three short questions will make the answer better.
steps.doesBehind: Reads the application already submitted. Does not re-ask anything it can already see.
steps.question: Happy to answer a few questions while this runs?

steps.showsCustomer: Your bank feed shows $412 a fortnight going to a card. Is the $9,400 the only balance you're consolidating?
steps.doesBehind: Reconciles declared debts against the bank feed. A mismatch here is the single most common reason an assessor sends an application back.
steps.question: Is that the only balance?

steps.showsCustomer: Your payslips and your bank feed disagree by about $180 a week. That's usually overtime. Is it regular?
steps.doesBehind: Flags the variance rather than silently choosing one figure. Which number is used changes the outcome, so the customer gets to explain it now instead of the assessor guessing later.
steps.question: Is the extra $180 regular?

steps.showsCustomer: Putting your file together. Nothing is decided yet.
steps.doesBehind: Drafts the affordability position and the suitability rationale against the Responsible Lending Code, with every figure traced to its source.

steps.approving: the affordability file and the suitability rationale, before any decision is formed
steps.showsCustomer: Your file is with a lending assessor. A person makes this call — that is not a formality, it is the law.
steps.doesBehind: Everything stops. The agent has no authority past this line.
steps.question: Release the file to the assessor?

steps.showsCustomer: Approved — $9,400 over 3 years. Here is what was counted, what was assumed, and who signed it.
steps.doesBehind: Writes the evidence pack: sources, assumptions, what the assessor changed, and the signature. One file the customer can keep or forward.

evidence.claim: 26% of shoppers abandon a checkout solely because the process was too long or complicated.
evidence.soWhat: The form is the friction. Moving the questions into a wait the customer is already having removes the form without removing the evidence.

evidence.claim: Making the work visible increases how much people value the result — across five experiments, users preferred a slower service that showed its effort.
evidence.source: Buell & Norton, “The Labor Illusion”, Management Science 57(9)
evidence.soWhat: A wait that shows its working is worth more than a wait that hides it. This is the whole argument for assembling.

evidence.claim: Compliance with the Responsible Lending Code is evidence of compliance with the lender responsibility principles.
evidence.soWhat: The rationale the agent drafts is written against the Code, so the file the assessor signs is already in the shape a regulator expects.

evidence.claim: Oversight of the CCCFA transferred to the Financial Markets Authority on 1 July 2026; certification was replaced by market-services licensing.
evidence.soWhat: A new regulator will ask how decisions were reached. An evidence pack per application is the cheapest possible answer.

evidence.claim: A tribunal held an airline liable for what its chatbot told a customer, rejecting the argument that the chatbot was a separate legal entity.
evidence.soWhat: This is why the assessor gate exists. An agent that could decide would be a liability, not a feature.

beforeWhileAfter.before: An eighteen-field form, submitted into silence. The assessor opens it, finds two gaps, and emails. Two days pass over a question that would have taken eight seconds to answer.
beforeWhileAfter.while: The wait becomes the assessment. Three short questions, asked one at a time, while the customer is still here and still interested. Every answer is traced to its source.
beforeWhileAfter.after: The assessor opens a complete file and signs it. The customer gets the reasoning, not just the verdict — and if the answer is no, they know exactly what would make it yes.

explainer.heading: what a monetised wait state actually is
explainer.standfirst: Nobody has a word for this yet, so here it is drawn out. Four panels, about a minute.
explainer.definition: A monetised wait state is a wait that pays for itself — you get something useful out of it, and the business gets work done that would otherwise cost it money later.

panels.title: the wait you already have
panels.caption: Every business makes people wait somewhere. Here it's the affordability check. Right now that time produces nothing for either side.

panels.title: what the gap costs
panels.caption: Some people give up while they wait. The same question gets asked twice. The work still happens later, and by then it costs more to do.

panels.title: what fills it
panels.caption: assembling puts useful work into the gap. One short question in, a complete file out — and something worth having handed back to you.

panels.title: who is better off
panels.caption: You finish sooner and can read the reasoning. The lender loses fewer applications and stops chasing by email. A lending assessor still signs it off.

textEquivalent: Start with the wait you already have. When you apply for a loan, there's a gap between sending the form and hearing back. Today nothing happens in that gap.
That gap costs money. Some people give up part-way. The same question gets asked twice, days apart. The work still gets done — later, by someone paid more to do it.
assembling fills the gap with useful work. It asks the smallest question that would improve the answer, and prepares the file while you wait.
By the end, both sides are better off: you get a decision you can read on the same day, and the lender gets a complete file instead of an email thread. A lending assessor signs it off, every time.
